steps.title: Count steps, not seconds
steps.caption: Reading a[5] takes 1 step at any n; a scan for a missing value takes n steps: 8, then 16.
steps.body: Big-O describes how the number of basic steps grows with the input size **n**, not the time on one machine. Reading `a[5]` by index touches one cell however long the array is, **O(1)**; searching an unsorted array for a value that isn't there checks every cell, **O(n)**. When the array doubles from 8 to 16 cells, the read still takes 1 step and the scan takes 16.

steps.title: Halving: O(log n)
steps.caption: Discarding half the sorted range each step takes 16 cells to 1 in 4 halvings; n = 32 needs just 5.
steps.body: On a sorted array, an algorithm that throws away half of the remaining range at every step goes 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: **4 halvings**, because log₂ 16 = 4. Doubling n to 32 adds only one more, so the curve rises quickly and then flattens. Binary search works this way, and so does a lookup in a balanced search tree.

steps.title: n log n and n²
steps.caption: Merge-sort levels fill 4 rows of 16 (64 steps); nested loops fill the whole 16 × 16 grid (256).
steps.body: Doing **n** work on each of **log₂ n** levels, as merge sort does, fills 4 rows of 16 cells: 64 steps. Comparing every item with every item in two nested loops fills the whole grid: 16 × 16 = 256 steps. On the chart, zoomed out 8×, the n log n curve stays inside the frame while n² leaves it.

steps.title: What it means at scale
steps.caption: At n = 1,000,000 and 10⁹ steps a second: O(n) takes 1 ms, O(n log n) 20 ms, O(n²) about 17 min.
steps.body: At **n = 1,000,000** the classes are worlds apart: 1 step, about 20, a million, about 20 million and a trillion. At an illustrative billion simple steps per second, the first two finish in nanoseconds, O(n) takes 1 ms, O(n log n) about 20 ms and O(n²) about **17 minutes**. Three rules keep Big-O simple: drop constant factors (3n + 5 is O(n)), keep the fastest-growing term (n² + n is O(n²)), and ignore the base of the logarithm.
